Perhaps the minister will permit me to make one or two observations with respect to this and the next item. As is
well known, this is a grant to an organization which for a long time was presided over by the most distinguished authority there was in Canada. This organization has been aided largely by a grant from a trust fund founded in the name of the mother of John D. Rockefeller, the Laura Spelman Rockefeller Memorial. The difficulty in connection with this work is that the citizens of the different provinces are now being compelled to pay large sums in taxation. I had made up my mind, for whatever it might be worth, that if a grant was to be given in connection with these matters it should be made to the provinces and not to the organizations, such as I have mentioned.
The organization concerned with this vote and that concerned with the following vote are doing a certain amount of propaganda work which is overlapped by the work of the provinces. Only the other day, the governor general pointed out in Montreal that his experience had been that great dangers arose from overlapping. The western provinces in particular have been carrying on an advanced work in this regard and the citizens of those provinces have to pay taxes so that the work can be carried out. As I said before, I had made up my mind that if we had to provide grants, we would give them to the provinces on some basis of fair distribution in order that those provinces which had the responsibility might have additional funds to enable them to do the work. My observation has been that the provinces are cramped very much in their work because of financial limitations.
We have one obligation cast upon us in the Victorian Order of Nurses. As hon. members know, this was founded by Lady Aberdeen and the country has given it assistance from the day of its establishment, as I hope it will long continue to do. Another obligation is placed upon us by article 25 of the peace treaty which reads:
The members of the league agree to encourage and promote the establishment and cooperation of duly authorized voluntary national Red Cross organizations having as purposes the improvement of health, the prevention of disease and the mitigation of suffering throughout the world.
There was difficulty in determining what national organization would be selected, but finally the Red Cross was selected. The work of the Red Cross has been most conducive to two things. First, there has been an improvement in the relations between children of the various countries of the world, and, second, there has been a steady improvement in health instruction. It would prove amaz-
Supply-National Health

ing to hon. members if they could see some of the communications that came from children in Japan to children in Alberta, and to see the contributions made by school children for the purpose of founding hospitals.
However, when it comes to these other matters of health education, to which I have referred as being obligations cast upon the provinces, I cannot but think that instead of maintaining an organization in the city of Toronto, for instance, where there would be a few officials receiving salaries, it would be much better to make a grant to the provinces. I had determined to do that, and I am bound to say that the representative of one of these organizations selected me as a target for his attacks on the theory that because I differed with him I must have some personal feeling in the matter. That is not the case; I have no interest beyond what I concede to be the public interest. In the case of many of these health organizations there is a duplication of activities which must rest upon the provincial authorities except to the extent mentioned by the minister. I repeat that moneys should be granted to the provinces to enable them more fittingly to discharge their duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say that my first reaction on entering the department and on looking over the grants to different organizations was somewhat similar to the conclusion arrived at by my right hon. friend. I am not so sure that I shall not eventually come to believe that these grants should be made directly to the provinces. The greatest difficulty is that organizations such as this one, being non-governmental, give the civilian or the non-professional man or the non-departmental person an opportunity to take part in the development of a particular work. However I feel there is a field open for extra departmental or governmental activity. Citizens who wish to be of some assistance to the community at large can join these associations and help to bring about some of the objects which it is desired to bring about. It is also possible to obtain subscriptions of public money which assist materially in the work. Apart from these considerations, I think the observations made by my right hon. friend are quite sound1. If I could get over that difficulty of not wishing to set aside the zeal of well-intentioned persons, I think I would agree heartily with him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am anxious to assist the minister in passing his estimates, but I should like to make one further observation. This item concerning mental hygiene was one
IMr. Bennett.]
in connection with which pressure was put upon the minister to include it in his estimates or the grant from the source I have indicated would be lost. That story has been told to successive governments. I am quite satisfied that that grant would be made to the provincial governments to enable them more fittingly to carry on their work.
On the second point, as long as taxation was moderate private benefactions were numerous, but men cannot now pay taxes and make benefactions at the same time. There is a field which used to be served entirely by private benefactions. For instance, hospitals in London are all maintained to-day by money that comes from endowments and private benefactions. The King Edward VII Hospital Fund has grown considerably; it has been contributed to from many sources, one of the largest being the contribution of Lord Mount Stephen, the first president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The point is that we must face the fact that the provinces are overburdened with taxation and that we cannot hope to obtain results by means of taxation upon and private benefactions from the same people, because they cannot give and at the same time pay taxes for the same thing. The relief afforded by the Income Tax Act with respect to ten per cent of income has enabled those who desire to make benefactions to do so and there has been a great improvement since that provision was made in the act.
It may sound strange, but the fact is that since the war, in Alberta the Red Cross has expended over $1,200,000 for the work mentioned in the article from which I have quoted. That money came from many sources, the head office, provincial grants, assistance from the municipalities, and private benefactions. These are becoming less and less; they are drying up because of the burden of taxation imposed upon individuals, which has become greater. In most of the provinces you find an income tax. They had an income tax in British Columbia before we had a federal income tax. They pay three taxes: income tax in the provinces, dominion income tax and municipal taxes, even school taxes sometimes. Therefore the matter has become very serious.
If the minister says that he is giving the matter consideration, looking it over in order to arrive at a conclusion, one can hardly expect him to have made his decisions with respect to these estimates, which had to be prepared so soon after his taking office. But on looking into the question I think he will conclude that the best interests of the country will be served by assisting those who are

Supply-National Health
charged with responsibility in this matter, because the federal Department of National Health can exist only if it is a coordinating influence between the various provinces and in the distribution of literature, coordinating all the activities of the provinces to secure some measure of uniformity in dealing with health problems. In discharging that true function of the Department of National Health it will be found that the department is serving the best interests of the dominion by encouraging the provinces, through financial assistance, in the great task which they have to perform in connection with public health.

I have one or two observations to make in reference to what the leader of the opposition has said. After all, these grants being made by the house are not sufficient to do any of the real work which the provinces are supposed to be doing. At the very most they can do only the very inefficient work of correlating the activities of the provincial organizations. I think there is a field for some central bureau at Ottawa not only in the sphere of child welfare but also in that of public health. I am not very much concerned whether the work is done through the provinces or through the dominion. I do not think there is any very clear indication that the British North America Act relegates public health work to the provinces; at any rate that is my reading of it. But I am more concerned about getting the work done. I can understand that a good many activities can be carried on better by the local authorities; but as the leader of the opposition has pointed out, the fact is that these local authorities are to-day practically bankrupt, and under these circumstances it seems to me that the dominion government ought to be making much larger grants either directly to the organizations or indirectly through subsidies to the provinces. I think the matter is most serious.
I glance down ten items in a block for these various philanthropic agencies dealing with public health and I find that the dominion government is contributing only a paltry $100,000. Two or three items further on I find in the estimate that, in order to assist in promoting the 'tourist business, an item $250,000 is granted, two and a half times as much. I have no particular objection to promoting the tourist business, but I do call attention to the fact that -that is more or less commercial. It may bring some money into the country and it benefits a great many people; but it does not touch nearly so closely the welfare of tens of thousands of our people as do these other items, and yet. so far as
the dominion is concerned, we are making no great provision for public health.
I do not want to go very fully into the matter to-night, but I think the time has come when the needs of the people across the country will have to be met more generously. Owing to the depression which has prevailed so long, about the only source from which we can hope to derive any assistance is the dominion government. I know it may be said that we ought to depend to a certain extent upon philanthropy, but private philanthropists have not come forward, and in any case it is a public obligation. It is a great deal better to tax people of great wealth than to leave the matter to voluntary contributions. We can be sure then that the money will come in; we are not sure at the present time.

I was glad to hear the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition. Personally I am doubtful whether any value is received for this grant, or in any case whether the value is sufficient. In Nova Scotia we have some very good sanatoria and in several of the towns we have tuberculosis annexes. There is no lack of public opinion as to the desirability of having tuberculosis patients looked after, but there is a tremendous lack of ability to have that done. I know that Nova Scotia provides a substantial sum, through the local legislature, and I also know that the municipalities make substantial contributions as well, but notwithstanding all that there are many patients who are unable to take advantage of the privileges of the sanatoria because that is beyond their means. A more substantial grant to the province would enable it in turn to reduce the charges to patients, and thus the privileges of the sanatoria would be placed within reach of those now unable to take advantage of them.

I also have no desire to hold up the estimates, but I should like to say a word following the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I do not know the situation in the two wealthy provinces of Quebec and Ontario, but certainly, as far as our western provinces are concerned, and possibly the maritime provinces as well, it is beyond our financial ability to care for the sick to the proper extent and degree. Instead of such grants as appear in these estimates to-night I believe there should be very much more substantial contributions; in fact, the provinces can hope to cope with sickness and

carry on properly only if they are given substantial grants. I do not think we will make any real headway at all in the western provinces, and possibly in other parts of Canada as well, unless the government can find some means of increasing our grants and, perhaps, of placing on the provinces the responsibility for the care of the sick.

You will note, Mr. Chairman, that these are all voluntary organizations. A good many of us have given this matter a great deal of consideration, and some of us are just wondering whether, instead of leaving the matter to voluntary organizations, this should not become a governmental responsibility. To-night I do not intend to do more than suggest to the minister that this matter is of such great importance that between now and next session, when probably he will be more familiar with his department, he should give serious consideration to the question whether the Department of National Health should not be reorganized to the extent necessary to take over these various activities. I recognize full well that these organizations have done a great deal of good. I recognize also that some of these organizations are carried on for propaganda work. But if it is necessary for voluntary organizations to carry on, and if this is the type of work that should be carried on, it seems to me that the time has come when we should recognize that as a national responsibility and give serious consideration to the question of taking it over as such.

I think we all recognize the fact that sometimes governments are slow to undertake new activities, and that from time to time excellent service is rendered to communities by public spirited ladies and gentlemen who form associations for the purpose of creating an intelligent public opinion to be brought to bear upon governments with respect to activities of the kind indicated, because governments await the pressure of public opinion before they act. The chief value I see in many of these organizations is the fact that they create a body of intelligent public opinion in favour of a line of action that may be desirable. We recall the action of one very wealthy gentleman in connection with one such activity in Ontario. He conceived the idea that manual training in the public schools would be advantageous, and for a number of years at his own expense he conducted manual training schools in several centres. Thus he demonstrated their value to such an extent that the province took over the work. I think that is an

Supply-National Health
illustration of the value of these organizations with which we have been dealing to-night.
Coming to the item under consideration, it seems to me that this organization has done its work so well that at the present time every provincial government in Canada is well aware of the importance of this work and the necessity for it, and every province has taken advanced measures along these lines. Perhaps the time has come when this organization has almost reached its objective. I quite agree with the remarks of the medical gentlemen who have just spoken; I believe the time has now come when the work of these organizations might be taken over either by the federal health department or by the provincial authorities on the representations of the federal department.

In this matter we might learn something from the developments that have taken place in connection with social work in some of our local communities. As a great many members well know we have often had a large number of charities spring up, fostered by this or that individual interested in some particular phase of social work. As the years have gone on sometimes these organizations have been found to overlap very seriously. Further than that, some of them, either through lack of trained workers or through the presence on their boards of people who have had not a wide range of knowledge, have distinctly lowered their standards. So it has been found necessary in many of our Canadian cities to create central boards. Those central boards try to correlate the various charitable agencies; they try as far as possible to raise the standard of treatment in these various agencies. In some instances they are entrusted with the task of advising the cities that make grants as to what grants may be given. This board will study the whole situation, study the budgets of the various institutions, the kind of work they are doing, and then will be better qualified to make those grants. We might fairly well undertake some such work as that here in Ottawa.
If, as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) has suggested, the department could be reorganized, it could perform two or three important functions. First, it could be a clearing house for information as to what is being done in the various provinces and through various departments. That in itself would be a valuable work. Then, if we are to enlarge our grants from the dominion, which policy I am glad to hear advocated by the leader of the opposition, it might very well be that to this bureau
would be entrusted more or less the investigation of the character of the work carried on by the different organizations and the different provinces. If the dominion government were making grants to provinces, to public health services, to tubercular services, they could insist on certain standards being maintained.
The Minister of Pensions suggested that he was desirous of retaining the services of volunteer workers, experts along these various lines. I think he might very well do that if he could appoint them in an advisory capacity on such a central board. We could have some one who was an expert in social hygiene, some one or some group expert in tuberculosis, or in child welfare. If we had half a dozen departments of this kind they would be in a position to give advice as to the lines along which we could advance. I think it must be admitted by anyone who is familiar with the work done in other countries that Canada has lagged, particularly in some departments, and that without the expenditure of too much money our own department could maintain this central bureau, which in turn would be in a position to advise with regard to the extension of the work throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I venture to suggest this to the consideration of the minister.

I have been
listening anxiously for many minutes to see if I could learn something about the work of the tuberculosis association, which I imagine is an anti-tuberculosis association. Could the minister give us the information, which has not been volunteered so far. as to how this money is used and its final disposition?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The association collects
money to finance campaigns in schools, in cities, in Indian reservations and generally throughout the dominion to educate the people in the care which should be taken in fighting tuberculosis. It also, as has been pointed out by the leader of the opposition, sells the anti-tuberculosis stamps which we receive at Christmas. The campaigns it puts on usually have for their object the education of 'the public on the subject of tuberculosis, the improvement of housing conditions and the establishment of sanatoria for the treatment of active cases. One of the most helpful measures is in continuing the local interest after the public addresses by distributing circulars, bulletins, et cetera, in the community. Also, it aids in the establishment of clinics.
Supply-National Health

It works through provincial anti-tuberculosis associations I
assume ?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Grant to the Canadian Dental Hygiene Council, $750.
Would the minister explain this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: This organization endeavours to interest the provincial authorities in dental hygiene and to educate the children in schools in dental care. As I understand the matter it goes from province to province; at the present time my information is that it is engaged in Ontario; last year it was in Prince Edward Island, I think. It arranges for lectures to the children in schools, and has a clinic to examine children and teach them the importance of dental hygiene.
Is there one individual engaged or only half an individual?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The provinces make grants; this is only to assist.

This is just a joke. If the dominion government representing ten million people grants only S750 to such an organization, I think the grant had better be cut out. If we are going into it we should go into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The total income is some $9,000 or more. The life insurance companies subscribe a certain amount. I will be frank in saying that this council have been asking for more money and will be very well pleased with the hon. member's observations in their behalf, but for this year we did not consider it possible to give them any more. But they are doing a useful work. I think the particular province in which they happen to be working in any year makes a grant that pretty nearly finances the work in that province; this money, I assume, would be devoted largely to the printing of pamphlets-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Purely clerical work.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: -and to purely clerical work in connection with their propaganda.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think I ought to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the minister found this item of $750 there and merely carried it on. The council sought a larger sum, as the minister explained. This sum is merely to assist with printing and clerical work, and is not intended to meet the large demands which under other circumstances they think should be made to meet the work in the provinces. I said to

them, as I say now, that ultimately any grants the dominion can make towards improving the teeth of the people, which is a provincial matter, should be made to the provinces themselves. Ontario carried on a travelling clinic which was one of the finest things I have ever seen. Then there was one operated by the Red Cross in Nova Scotia which was most successful, and one year I think there was one operating in Manitoba ; I am not sure of that. This small grant is simply to indicate that they are worthy of recognition.

But it does not indicate that; I should say that the smallness of the grant indicates that they are a pretty poor outfit. When we consider that in nearly all our larger cities they have clinics in the public schools and that in many provinces there are travelling clinics doing dental work among the children, it seems to me absurd that the dominion government should give so little. I think the minister might give S80 or $90 to each province, and let them take over the work. Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In all probability the provinces would not have made the advances which have been made in the work had it not been for the association, one which to a great extent is financed by the insurance companies. In Quebec the work is being attended to by the sanitary units or, as we describe them, les unites sanitaires. But assistance is required from the dental hygiene council, and possibly some guidance could be given as to the methods of carrying out the work most effectively. I agree that the amount is not very great, and were it within my power to give more I -would gladly do so. I shall make representations, and see that the hon. member's, representations are carried to the Minister of Finance in the hope that his heart may melt a little, and that he may give an extra $250.

May I commend the words of the minister and the work the organization is doing. I believe it is doing even more than the minister has indicated. I have known this organization through its director, Doctor Thompson, to go into a municipality and encourage it to undertake the survey of children in schools in order to ascertain the dental work which might be required. It has been doing a work which is of tremendous value to that municipality.
May I supplement the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre by stating that if the grant could be increased the efficiency of th.e organization would be improved to a great extent. It would be doing work such as that suggested earlier in the

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Questions
evening, namely, that of helping the child who is unable to help himself. We know that, if not properly cared for, teeth may be the cause of illness. The organization is attempting to remedy defects of that kind, not only by itself, but through existing organizations. May I offer every encouragement possible to the minister in his efforts to secure a larger grant for the organization?

Before we leave the
medical items there are some matters I should like to bring to the attention of the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member speaking to this item?
I shall speak about medical matters, but there is no such item in the estimates. The minister may carry the item if he likes, so long as I am permitted to speak for a moment or two afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The hon. member will have an opportunity to speak under the item for administration.
Did I understand the minister to say that the association, bureau, or w'atever it is, prints articles or pamphlets on dental hygiene?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.

Would he mind sending a few to his colleague the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs? The dental hygiene among Indian children has been much neglected. In late years, for the sake of economy if you like to put it in that way, they have got it down to little else but pulling out those teeth which are in a bad state of decay. That is not true economy. The Indian agent tells me that since that policy was adopted hospital bills have increased in our damp British Columbia climate, and that the Indians have had to have more treatment for diseased glands, tonsils and the like. It is recognized generally that it is more economical to take care of the teeth, and to treat them in the initial stage of decay * rather than to resort to pulling them out when they get beyond saving.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I shall be pleased to see that the superintendent general receives two or three pamphlets.

speechtext: Item agreed to.
